newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BEUC calls for new EU rules on child advertising.
newsitem.headline: BEUC calls for new EU rules on child advertising.

text.p: European consumer organisations on Monday urged the European Union to legislate to protect children from increasingly diverse and devious methods of advertising.

"Children are subjected to commercial pressure in almost every aspect of their daily lives: on television...at the sports club, playing games, eating breakfast, on their way to school, at school," said Jim Murray, Director of consumer lobby BEUC.
"However, children do not have the same capacity to understand the commercial aim behind these marketing practices as adults do and therefore are more vulnerable."

Murray, commenting in a statement on the results of a pan-European survey on children between the ages of six and 12 and advertising, said it was becoming increasingly difficult even for adults to identify advertising, let alone children.

The study shows that both national and EU regulation has failed to keep up with increasingly more sophisticated and often more covert marketing techniques, said BEUC, which groups national consumer organisations.

It said the techniques involve in-school marketing, children's clubs, contests, sponsorship of children's events, direct mail, teleshopping, offering free gifts, and promoting a product by linking it to a favourite children's movie or toy.
The group said that even where they could spot the advertising children would not be able to develop a questionning attitude until they were 11 or 12 years of age.
In particular, BEUC said it was seeking restrictions on in-school marketing and direct marketing.

They said the legislation should establish the principle whereby a member state with more stringent requirements could apply those provisions to marketing practices on its territory originating from another member state.
The increase of new forms of advertising, notably through the internet and the new information highways make action in this field even more urgent, it said.
